questions.q: Define situational irony and give one example from "Glory at Twilight" where the outcome of an action is the opposite of what the character intended.
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when the result of an action is contrary to the intended or expected effect. In the story, Satyajit attends the wedding to briefly reclaim his former status and give a modest gift (Rs 101), but the situational irony is that he is coerced into signing away his ancestral house and fish-pond—the very assets he meant to preserve for his wife and son—thereby losing his last tangible security while performing the role of a generous benefactor. A wrong answer (e.g., citing the train's unauthorised stops) reveals confusion between mere inconvenience and structural irony where character agency backfires.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the title "Glory at Twilight" functions as a symbol rather than a mere description of the time of day. What abstract concept does it compress?
questions.a: The title symbolises the fleeting, borrowed splendour Satyajit experiences during the wedding day—twilight is the brief, borrowed light after sunset, just as his "glory" is a borrowed reflection of past wealth that villagers still project onto him. It compresses the theme of illusory status: the glory is real in the villagers' eyes but already dead in reality, much like twilight mimics daylight while darkness advances. A wrong answer that treats "twilight" only as the wedding's evening timing misses the symbolic layering and fails to connect to the story's central tension between appearance and reality.

questions.q: Apply the concept of dramatic irony to the scene where Uncle Srinath introduces Satyajit as a "millionaire" and "pride of Bengal." What does the reader know that the villagers do not, and how does this gap create tension?
questions.a: The reader knows Satyajit's bank has collapsed, his assets are gone, and he has only Rs 200 in his purse, while the villagers believe he is a wealthy industrialist. This dramatic irony creates tension because every accolade ("son of Bengal," "god on the pedestal") tightens the trap: the higher they lift him, the harder his inevitable fall when the cash demand arrives. The tension peaks when Srinath demands Rs 2001 "as a drop in the ocean"—the reader watches Satyajit's internal calculation (saving Rs 50 for a perambulator) clash with the villagers' fantasy. A wrong answer that merely lists the praise without contrasting it with Satyajit's hidden poverty shows inability to track the knowledge gap that defines dramatic irony.

questions.q: Analyse how the fish-pond operates as a multi-layered symbol across three different moments in the story. What does it represent in each context?
questions.a: First, the pond symbolises Satyajit's rooted identity and childhood security when he visits it ("This small house gave him a feeling of security which had not come to him even from his huge city mansion"). Second, it becomes a symbol of auspicious continuity when the caught carp is designated for the bride and groom's midnight feast ("bring them all the blessings that life can give"). Third, it transforms into a symbol of sacrificial dignity when Satyajit signs it over to the moneylender—his final act of "benediction" that strips him of the last asset he intended for his wife. The pond thus traces the arc from personal sanctuary to communal ritual to tragic surrender. A wrong answer that only notes "it is his property" fails to track the symbol's evolving thematic weight across the narrative.

questions.q: Evaluate the author's choice to use verbal irony in Satyajit's internal monologue ("What now?" repeated as an obsession) versus the verbal irony in Uncle Srinath's speeches. Which is more effective in revealing the story's central conflict, and why?
questions.a: Satyajit's internal "What now?" is a bitter, recursive verbal irony—he asks a question he cannot answer, and the repetition underscores his helplessness; it reveals the psychological conflict of a man who defined himself by control now facing uncontrollable collapse. Srinath's verbal irony ("benediction" meaning cash, "millionaire's signature" worth less than a pond) is performative, weaponising respect to extract money. Satyajit's internal irony is more effective for the central conflict because it exposes the protagonist's fracture between self-image and reality, while Srinath's irony merely externalises the predatory social structure. A wrong answer that treats both as equally "ironic dialogue" misses the distinction between character-revealing internal irony and plot-driving external irony.

questions.q: Create a new symbolic object for a hypothetical sequel set five years later, where Satyajit has rebuilt a modest life. Describe the object, its literal function, and the abstract idea it would compress—mirroring how the fish-pond functioned in the original story.
questions.a: Object: A second-hand bicycle Satyajit buys to commute to his new clerkship. Literal function: daily transport, economy, independence from erratic trains. Symbolic compression: the bicycle's two wheels echo the "wheel of fortune" motif—now human-powered, not fate-driven; its steady forward motion represents agency regained; the fact that it is second-hand mirrors his acceptance of reduced circumstances without shame. A poor answer would pick an object with no thematic resonance (e.g., a new pen) or fail to link the object's physical properties to the story's established motifs (wheel, motion, ownership, dignity).
